issues.title: D28: VVIX and OVX fail not_a_csv (Cboe two-column file)
issues.summary: The Cboe vol indexes arrive as a two-column file, but the D28 vol-index input still parses the one-column shape, so every VVIX and OVX pull fails with not_a_csv.

detail.whats_wrong: VVIX and OVX are published by Cboe as a two-column file (date, value). The D28 vol-index input asks its CSV reader for the single-column shape, so each pull of either index ends in not_a_csv and the day never reaches the store.
detail.evidence: module_earnings_radar/inputs/vol_index.py:28,33 writes vol_index_daily; nothing reads that table yet (only the schema at core/rawstore.py:1841 and the series list at core/automations.py:193). The consumers are the unbuilt ROT-4 vol panel (Sector Rotation) and SPX-7 (SPX Gamma).
detail.example: A VVIX request for one session returns the Cboe page with a header row and two columns; the parse rejects it, so vol_index_daily keeps the previous day.
detail.direction: Teach the reader the two-column Cboe layout (date, value) and keep the one-column path for the other indexes, before ROT-4 and SPX-7 start reading the table.
detail.next_step: Fix the parser in module_earnings_radar/inputs/vol_index.py against a stored Cboe response, then re-run the D28 input check.

issues.title: D28: MOVE fails no_bars (bare ticker where a sequence is expected)
issues.summary: The MOVE index is asked for as a bare ticker while the vol-index path expects a sequence, so the D28 input fails with no_bars instead of storing a row.

detail.whats_wrong: MOVE is fetched through the vol-index path, which expects a price sequence per session. The input asks for the bare ticker ^MOVE, gets a single quote back and reports no_bars, so no MOVE row is written.
detail.evidence: module_earnings_radar/inputs/vol_index.py:34-35 sets MOVE_TICKER = "^MOVE" and feeds the same writer as VVIX and OVX; the table is vol_index_daily, which no board reads yet.
detail.example: A MOVE pull for one date returns one quote object rather than a bar sequence, and the input records no_bars for that date.
detail.direction: Either ask the provider for a bar sequence for MOVE or accept the single quote and write it as that session's value; the choice belongs with the provider seam, not the writer.
detail.next_step: Decide the shape in the issue, then adjust the MOVE branch of vol_index.py and add a fixture for each shape.

issues.title: D27: non-JSON FRED body reported only as JSONDecodeError
issues.summary: When FRED answers with an HTML error page instead of JSON, the input reports a bare JSONDecodeError, which hides the status code and the reason the macro series is missing.

detail.whats_wrong: A FRED request that comes back with a non-JSON body (an HTML error page, a redirect notice) is decoded straight, so the failure reaches the operator as JSONDecodeError with no status and no series name.
detail.evidence: The FRED macro series feed Earnings Radar and Sector Rotation (see the cross-board seam in public #13), so one unreadable body blanks the macro rows of two boards at once.
detail.example: A 502 from the FRED host returns an HTML page; the input logs JSONDecodeError and the run continues with no macro series, with nothing saying which request failed.
detail.direction: Check the content type and the status before decoding, and report the series id, the status and the first characters of the body in a provider-shaped error.
detail.next_step: Add the status/content-type guard to the FRED reader and a fixture with an HTML body; assert the message names the series and the status.

issues.title: DuckDB 4.3 GiB temp ceiling in the 13F derive
issues.summary: The SEC 13F derive spills past DuckDB's 4.3 GiB temp-file ceiling on the real store, so the full derive cannot finish without changing how the intermediates are built.

detail.whats_wrong: The 13F derive sorts and joins intermediates that do not fit DuckDB's 4.3 GiB temp ceiling on the real store. The derive stops instead of completing, so totals cannot be rebuilt from the ingested data sets on this machine.
detail.evidence: The failing run and its temp-file ceiling are recorded in the issue; the derive is driven by scripts/migrate_sec13f_v12.py, which is also the script public #10 reports.
detail.example: A derive over the full ingested data set reaches the temp ceiling and aborts before writing the totals, leaving the board on the previous derive.
detail.direction: Investigate the size and shape of the intermediates first (which join spills, how many rows), then choose between a narrower projection, a different join order, or a temp directory with room.
detail.next_step: Reproduce the derive with the spill accounted for, record peak temp usage in the issue, then decide the fix.

issues.title: migrate_sec13f_v12 docstring and --derive-only swallow a refusal
issues.summary: scripts/migrate_sec13f_v12.py documents a behaviour it does not have, and its --derive-only flag turns a refused derive into a quiet success.

detail.whats_wrong: The script's docstring describes the migration one way while the code does another, and --derive-only continues after a refusal, so a caller sees exit 0 although nothing was derived.
detail.evidence: The mismatch is between the module docstring and the --derive-only branch of scripts/migrate_sec13f_v12.py; the derive it wraps is the one public #9 reports as hitting the temp ceiling.
detail.example: Running the script with --derive-only on a derive that refuses prints no failure and exits 0, so an operator believes the totals were rebuilt.
detail.direction: Make the refusal raise (or exit non-zero) and correct the docstring to the actual steps the script performs.
detail.next_step: Add a test that a refusing derive exits non-zero under --derive-only, then fix the flag and the docstring.

issues.title: 13F: large well-known issuers stay unmatched in the derive
issues.summary: 99.7% of the $3,996.89B left out of the newest period was asked of OpenFIGI and came back with no ticker, so large issuers are missing from the stored 13F totals.

detail.whats_wrong: The derive leaves out CUSIPs whose OpenFIGI answer carries no ticker, including large well-known holdings, because an empty answer is stored without the reason it was empty.
detail.evidence: 10,297 CUSIPs / $3,996.89B (2026-06-30); 14,656 present vs 15,428 absent, all from the 2026-10-15 run; module_sec_13f/engine.py:1028-1065.
detail.example: Exxon Mobil, CUSIP 30231G102: $354.43B held, identity_cusip.status = absent, source = openfigi, empty ticker; the board shows roughly $6-7B for XOM.
detail.tried_or_decided: Logged as an open known problem on 2026-10-22, deliberately not built before Sunday 25 Oct.
detail.direction: 1) record WHY an answer was empty in identity_cusip.status; 2) retry the empty answers with a name query; 3) prefer the SEC's own issuer name to confirm a match; 4) owner decision on non-US-domiciled lines.
detail.next_step: Write the follow-up brief after Sunday 25 Oct, starting from the status values the next derive records.

issues.title: ROTATION_ETFS is reference data living in a board module
issues.summary: The ETF reference list is defined inside the Sector Rotation board module but imported by the app runners and by Relatedness, so a board owns shared data.

detail.whats_wrong: ROTATION_ETFS is reference data (a fixed ETF list with its names) that lives in a board package, yet two other layers import it, so the board module is a dependency of the app and of another board.
detail.evidence: Defined at module_sector_rotation/universe.py:10; imported by app/runners.py:552,1095 and module_relatedness/themes.py:1038,1090.
detail.direction: Move the list to a shared reference-data home (next to the index registry and the GICS map) and have the board, the runners and Relatedness import it from there.
detail.next_step: Pick the destination module in the issue, then move the constant with its ETF labels and update the three importers.

issues.title: Earnings Radar and Sector Rotation import each other
issues.summary: Earnings Radar and Sector Rotation import each other for the macro series, so neither board can be read, moved or tested without the other.

detail.whats_wrong: The macro weekly closes are defined on one board and consumed by the other, and the import runs both ways, so the two board packages form a cycle.
detail.evidence: The shared names are MACRO_SERIES and macro_weekly_closes, used by both board packages.
detail.direction: Move the macro series definition and its reader into one shared input module, then have both boards import that instead of each other.
detail.next_step: Map the two import directions in the issue, then move the smaller side first and drop the back-import.

issues.title: CFTC COT parse is reached through two private SPX Gamma helpers
issues.summary: The CFTC COT writer lives in Earnings Radar but parses its rows through two private SPX Gamma helpers, so one board reaches into another's internals.

detail.whats_wrong: The COT input writes its rows through helpers that are private to the SPX Gamma board, which makes an implemented input depend on another board's module surface.
detail.evidence: The writer is module_earnings_radar/inputs/cftc_cot.py; the parse helpers it calls live in the SPX Gamma package.
detail.direction: Move the parse helpers into a shared input module that both boards import, and delete the private copies from SPX Gamma.
detail.next_step: Name the two helpers in the issue, then move them with their tests and update both callers.

issues.title: Financials board computes Asymmetric Growth's score
issues.summary: The Financials board computes the Asymmetric Growth score inside its own render path, so a screener's rule is owned by a different board.

detail.whats_wrong: The growth score is calculated in the Financials board's code, which means the screener's rule has two owners and a change to the score touches a board that does not own it.
detail.evidence: The score computation sits in the Financials board; Asymmetric Growth is the board that displays and tests it (see the screener epic private #380).
detail.direction: Move the score computation into the Asymmetric Growth package (or a shared screener module) and have Financials call it.
detail.next_step: List the functions Financials calls for the score in the issue, then move them and keep the Financials output byte-identical.

issues.title: Asymmetric Growth engine imports the SEC 13F engine
issues.summary: The Asymmetric Growth engine imports the SEC 13F engine for shared helpers, so the screener stops working whenever the 13F package changes shape.

detail.whats_wrong: A screener engine imports another board's engine module, which makes the screener depend on the 13F package's internals rather than on a shared contract.
detail.evidence: The import is in the Asymmetric Growth engine; the 13F package it reaches is the one carrying the known problem in public #11.
detail.direction: Move the helpers the screener needs into a shared module (identity or store level) and drop the engine-to-engine import.
detail.next_step: Name the imported helpers in the issue, then extract them with their tests.

issues.title: core/models/ holds two single-board model modules
issues.summary: core/models/ holds one model module per single board, so a shared package carries board code that only Earnings Radar or Sector Rotation reads.

detail.whats_wrong: The two model modules under core/models/ are each read by exactly one board, so the shared core carries board-specific logic and the board's own package does not own its model.
detail.evidence: core/models/ holds exactly events.py (Earnings Radar only) and rotation.py (Sector Rotation only).
detail.direction: Move each model module into the board package that reads it, and keep only genuinely shared models in core/models/.
detail.next_step: Move events.py and rotation.py with their imports in one change, then delete the empty shared surface.

issues.title: The screeners' machinery lives in core/ (six files)
issues.summary: Six screener modules live in core/, so the three screener boards share machinery through the core package instead of through a screener layer of their own.

detail.whats_wrong: The screener rules, scoring and gates are filed under core/ rather than under the three boards that use them, so core/ grows with screener work and the boards own none of it.
detail.evidence: Six files under core/ serve only Asymmetric Growth, Swing Potential and Fundamentals.
detail.direction: Give the screeners a shared package (or move each file into the board that owns it) and keep core/ for cross-board concerns.
detail.next_step: List the six files and their readers in the issue, then move them in one reviewed change.

issues.title: Platform: job deadline/cancel, progress + run log, writer locks, schema check, credential gating
issues.summary: The job machinery every board's Fetch runs on still lacks deadlines, cancel, progress with a run log, writer locks, a schema check and credential gating.

detail.whats_wrong: A Fetch is a queued job, and the platform around it is only partly built: no deadline or cancel per job, no progress with a run log, no writer locks, no schema check and no credential gate before a run starts.
detail.evidence: Every board's Fetch goes through the same job queue in app/dashboard.py, so a gap here shows on all 16 boards at once.
detail.direction: Land the items one at a time behind their own tests, starting with the deadline and cancel pair, which already have a partial surface in app/tests.
detail.next_step: Split the issue into one slice per item and mark which are already shipped.

issues.title: Job lock: a PID we cannot open keeps the lock held
issues.summary: The job lock treats a process id it is not allowed to inspect as still running, so the lock stays held and every board's Fetch waits on a dead owner.

detail.whats_wrong: When the lock's recorded PID cannot be opened (permission denied), the liveness check cannot prove the process is gone, so it assumes it is alive and keeps the lock.
detail.evidence: The lock is the one every board's Fetch takes (core/job_lock.py); the stale-lock breakers are the other half in private #365.
detail.example: A dashboard left over from an elevated session leaves a lock whose PID the next user cannot open; the next Fetch never starts.
detail.direction: Treat an unopenable PID as unknown rather than alive, and let the age-based breaker decide, with the reason logged.
detail.next_step: Add a test with an unopenable PID, then change the liveness verdict to three-valued.

issues.title: Job lock: two breakers of one stale lock can both hold it
issues.summary: Two processes can break the same stale job lock at once and each believe it holds the lock, so two Fetches run together over the same store.

detail.whats_wrong: Breaking a stale lock is not atomic: both breakers see the stale file, both remove it and both create their own, so the mutual exclusion the lock exists for is lost.
detail.evidence: Same lock as private #364: every board's Fetch takes it, and the store underneath allows one writer.
detail.example: Two dashboards start on the same store after a crash; both break the stale lock and both run a Fetch, and the second writer hits the store lock.
detail.direction: Break the stale lock with one atomic step (rename or compare-and-swap on the file) so exactly one breaker wins.
detail.next_step: Write the two-breaker test first, then make the break atomic.

issues.title: Inputs: every dashboard data request (D01-D37)
issues.summary: The inputs epic tracks the D01-D37 data requests behind every board, and it stays open while any request row is still unfinished or failing.

detail.whats_wrong: This epic carries the input rows D01-D37 that the boards consume. It is unfinished: the request rows themselves are the count of what is still open, and the failing ones are filed next to it (for example the VVIX/OVX, MOVE and FRED rows in public #6, #7 and #8).
detail.evidence: The three public input bugs already filed against rows of this epic are public #6 (VVIX and OVX), #7 (MOVE) and #8 (FRED body).
detail.direction: Keep one row per input with its store table, its writer and its consumers, and close the epic when every row has a passing check.
detail.next_step: Mark the completed rows in the issue body and list the remaining ones.

issues.title: Common: shared work found in the dashboard reviews
issues.summary: The shared-UI epic collects the cross-board work found in the dashboard reviews; this open-issues panel is one of its items.

detail.whats_wrong: This epic carries the shared chrome and contract work that individual board reviews keep finding: the filter kit, the help box, the provider banner, the recorded-sessions block, the payload route and now the open-issues panel. It stays open until the remaining review items are closed.
detail.evidence: The panel delivered with this registry is an item of this epic; core/reporting_common.py and docs/dashboard_ui.md are its two homes.
detail.direction: Keep one item per shared component, each with its own guard test, so a board cannot fork it.
detail.next_step: List the remaining review findings in the issue and close them one slice at a time.

issues.title: Theme naming: duplicate names get a member label appended
issues.summary: Two themes with the same name get a member label appended to tell them apart, so the Theme cascade of every equity board shows labels like Transportation and Logistics (Aax).

detail.whats_wrong: When the pinned run produces two coarse themes with the same name, the catalog disambiguates them by appending a member label in parentheses. The label is derived from a holding rather than from the theme, so it reads as nonsense in a filter.
detail.evidence: Theme labels come from relatedness_themes through core/universe.py:190-214 theme_catalog() and reach the Theme cascade of every equity board's filter bar via reporting_common.filters_meta (:130-141).
detail.example: The Theme dropdown shows "Transportation and Logistics (Aax)" beside "Transportation and Logistics".
detail.direction: Disambiguate with a stable suffix that describes the theme (its id or its top weight) rather than one member ticker's label.
detail.next_step: Reproduce the duplicate in the pinned run, then change the suffix rule in theme_catalog() and its filter test.

issues.title: Structure A: area map, plans index and the misplaced seams
issues.summary: Structure A is the area map, the plans index and the misplaced-seam list the public seam issues work through, and it stays open until the map is accurate.

detail.whats_wrong: The repository has no single area map that says which package owns what, so the seam issues keep being discovered one by one instead of being read off a map.
detail.evidence: docs/system_map.md is the map; the public seam issues #12-#18 are the misplaced seams it should list.
detail.direction: Keep docs/system_map.md and a plans index current, and list every known seam there with a link to its issue.
detail.next_step: Add the seam table to docs/system_map.md and link each public seam issue.

issues.title: Storage: confirm no double-encoded JSON cells remain
issues.summary: Some store cells may still hold JSON encoded twice, so a reader that decodes once returns a string where the rest of the code expects an object.

detail.whats_wrong: A double-encoded JSON cell decodes to a string that looks like JSON. Readers that decode once then index the result fail or silently see text, and the fault shows up as a board quirk rather than a storage bug.
detail.evidence: This is a store-wide check across the typed and JSON columns described in docs/data_architecture.md.
detail.example: A history params cell holding a quoted JSON object decodes to a str, so the recorded-sessions row prints the whole object as its params text.
detail.direction: Scan every JSON column once with a decode-twice check, fix the writers that double-encode, and add a guard for new ones.
detail.next_step: Write the scan as a script, record its findings in the issue, and fix the writers it names.

issues.title: Final pass: core and health ledger
issues.summary: The final-pass epic covers the core clean-up and the data-health ledger; it remains open while its remaining slices are unbuilt.

detail.whats_wrong: This epic carries the closing pass over core/ and the data-health ledger. Its remaining slices are the count of what is still open; they are listed in the epic's own checklist.
detail.evidence: The ledger work is described in docs/data_health.md; the core slices are the moves tracked by private #45.
detail.direction: Close the slices in the order the epic lists them, each with its own test.
detail.next_step: Re-read the epic's checklist and mark which slices have landed.

issues.title: Backlog: ideas parked as "not now"
issues.summary: The parked backlog holds the ideas deliberately set aside as not now, kept in one place so the roadmaps do not carry them.

detail.whats_wrong: Ideas that are not being built need one home, otherwise they either clutter the area epics or get lost.
detail.evidence: The issue carries the parked list; entries leave it only when an area epic adopts one.
detail.tried_or_decided: Parked on purpose: the ideas are recorded, not scheduled.
detail.direction: Adopt an entry by moving it into its area epic, and keep this list for ideas nobody has scheduled.
detail.next_step: Re-read the list when a roadmap round starts and move anything that now fits an area.
